Neonatal Common chuckwallas (Sauromalus ater) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a snout-vent length (SVL) of 7.0 centimeters [Lb = 7.0 centimeters], a measurement that positions them among the larger-bodied hatchlings within the Iguanidae. The wet weight of these newly emerged individuals averages 7.5 grams [Wwb = 7.5 grams], though field data indicate a natural range extending from approximately 6 to 9.6 grams, reflecting variation in yolk reserves and maternal provisioning. This modest mass at hatching belies the substantial growth trajectory the species undertakes, as these young reptiles must navigate a challenging desert environment. The transition from lecithotrophic dependence to active foraging occurs shortly after emergence, marking the onset of exogenous feeding. In the Sonoran and Mojave deserts where this species is endemic, neonatal survivorship is closely tied to the timing of the summer monsoon rains, which drive the availability of the herbaceous plants and succulent perennials that constitute the primary diet.

Reproductive output in the Common chuckwalla is constrained by the arid thermal regimes of its habitat. Under stable laboratory conditions maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate reaches approximately 0.022 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 0.022 offspring per day], a figure that translates to roughly eight offspring produced annually per reproductively active female. This moderate fecundity is characteristic of a K-selected life-history strategy typical of large-bodied desert lizards. While individual females may produce only a single clutch per year in many wild populations, the potential for higher output under optimal thermal conditions suggests that temperature plays a critical role in regulating vitellogenesis and egg formation. The timing of reproduction is synchronized with the brief spring period of vegetative productivity, ensuring that neonates have access to sufficient forage during their critical first months of life.

Sexual maturation in this species exhibits a pronounced dimorphism. Males attain puberty at a snout-vent length of 12.5 centimeters [Lp = 12.5 centimeters], a smaller body size compared to females, which typically do not reach reproductive maturity until they achieve an SVL of approximately 13.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 13.5 centimeters]. This divergence is consistent with patterns observed across many iguanid lizards, in which males mature earlier to secure territories and access to females before they have completed somatic growth. The ecological implication is that male chuckwallas begin competing for mates and defending rocky retreats at a younger age, often engaging in conspicuous push-up displays and lateral compression postures to intimidate rivals. Females, by contrast, delay reproduction to accumulate the body reserves necessary for egg production, a strategy that enhances clutch viability in a resource-limited environment.

The ultimate body size achieved by adult Common chuckwallas reveals a clear sexual size dimorphism favoring males. The maximum recorded snout-vent length for the species overall is 18.6 centimeters [Li = 18.6 centimeters], but when sexes are considered separately, males surpass this average, reaching an ultimate SVL of 19.9 centimeters [Li = 19.9 centimeters]. This larger adult size in males is likely an adaptation for intrasexual combat, as larger individuals enjoy a competitive advantage in defending the basking sites and crevice refuges critical for thermoregulation. The egg-hatching event marks the beginning of a lengthy growth period that spans several years before asymptotic size is approached. Growth rates in the wild are highly variable, influenced by annual fluctuations in precipitation and the quality of herbaceous forage. Adult chuckwallas are robust, heavily built lizards whose body mass can exceed 500 grams in prime individuals.

Longevity data for Sauromalus ater, derived from both mark-recapture studies and captive observations, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3,395 days [am = approximately 3,395 days] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], a figure equivalent to roughly 9.3 years. This extended lifespan is notable among desert lizards and reflects a slow metabolic pace and low predation pressure in adults, which are well protected by their rugged dermal armor and habit of wedging themselves into rock crevices. Natural mortality in the wild is concentrated in the first year of life, when young chuckwallas are vulnerable to predation by snakes, raptors, and mammalian carnivores. Survivorship improves dramatically once individuals reach a body size sufficient to exploit crevice refuges.
